subject: Anthropology
title: Sociolinguistics
description: A quick, practical guide to Sociolinguistics.

hook.text: You speak differently to your boss than to your best friend. Your language shifts to match the social moment.

buildup.text: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies across social groups and situations — class, gender, age, and region.

discovery.text: William Labov showed that even small pronunciation differences signal social class in places like New York City.

twist.text: There's no correct dialect — only prestigious ones. Standard language is a political choice, not a linguistic one.

climax.text: How you speak reveals where you're from, who you know, and where you sit in the social hierarchy.

punchline.text: Every accent tells a social story.

quiz.question: What did Labov's research demonstrate?
options: All people speak identically in cities

details.summary: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies by social group — class, gender, age, ethnicity, and region. Speech patterns signal social identity and are evaluated by listeners, with standard dialects typically receiving prestige while non-standard varieties face stigma.
details.whyItMatters: Language variation is never random — it maps onto social hierarchies. Understanding sociolinguistic variation reveals how language reinforces inequality and how speech marks social identity in every interaction.
takeaways: Language varies systematically by class, gender, age, and region
Speech patterns signal and construct social identity
Standard dialects receive prestige while others face stigma

faq.question: Are some dialects linguistically inferior to others?
faq.answer: No. All dialects are equally systematic and complex from a linguistic perspective. Standard dialects gain prestige through political and economic power, not linguistic superiority. What is considered correct speech is a social judgment, not a scientific one.

faq.question: How does speech signal social class?
faq.answer: Accent, vocabulary, grammar, and conversational style all signal class position. William Labov's studies showed that New York department store workers in higher-end stores produced more prestige pronunciations. Speakers unconsciously adjust speech to signal or claim social position.
